item.title: A specter is haunting North America
item.description: 200 years ago, our ancestors thought spots on the sun brought winter in June.
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Jerusalem Demsas

In the summer of 1816, it snowed in New England. Across the Atlantic, Europeans still reeling from the end of the Napoleonic Wars saw their continent descend into a science-fiction nightmare.

“The inhabitants of Taranto, in southern Italy, were terrified by red and yellow snowflakes in a place where even normal snow was a rarity. Brown, bluish, and red snow fell in Maryland in April and May. Everywhere, the dust hung in a dry fog,” recounted anthropologist Brian Fagan in 2000.

Writing in 1984, NASA scientist Richard Stothers described the root cause of the bizarre climatic event: a volcanic eruption in Indonesia that exceeded “any other known eruption, historical or otherwise, during the past 10,000 years.”

The ash that blanketed the globe caused the mean temperature in the Northern Hemisphere to drop between 0.4 and 0.7 degrees Celsius. To put this into context for our climate-conscious readers: the Tambora eruption temporarily reversed, in a single year, the equivalent of roughly one-third to one-half of all the warming humanity has caused since the Industrial Revolution.1

I thought back to this 200-year-old atmospheric event on Friday, when I walked outside and breathed in a lungful of smoke.

It’s nice to live in a time when what can only be described as an apocalyptic haze is quickly explained by dozens of scientists and newspapers. Unlike our unfortunate 19th-century ancestors, we know what’s going on; they instead were forced to bandy about batty theories about sunspots blocking sunlight, wind patterns, and the amount of gunpowder discharged during the Napoleonic Wars.

Share

The proximate causes of our modern apocalyptic haze are the hundreds of fires blazing across Canada, many of which are in “remote, northernmost reaches of Ontario, where there are no highways, roads or people.”

Smoke inhalation is often an ancillary part of a broadly pleasurable activity — at a campfire, while cooking a meal indoors, or as a vehicle for imbibing nicotine or marijuana. It can be easy to ignore the fact that you are slowly reducing your life expectancy.

It’s almost hard to believe the current state of the research, because if you take it at face value, you’re forced to conclude that it’s impossible to overrate the importance of air quality. According to a report by Founders Pledge, “Air pollution is the fifth largest risk factor for mortality” worldwide, responsible for nearly 7 million deaths every year. The report added that 99% of the world’s population lives in areas with poor air quality.2

Beyond the mortality impacts, poor air quality makes you dumber, poorer, and maybe even more depressed (though the evidence here is more mixed). Time and again, research on air quality reveals its myriad negative impacts:

Economists found that when the wind blows pollution from refineries, corn milling facilities, and foundries into specific Chicago neighborhoods, crime goes up. They found that air pollution increases violent crime but not property crime, “consistent with research from biology and medicine linking air pollution and aggression.”

During the pandemic, there was a brief surge of concern about air quality: The U.S. portable air-treatment market grew 57% in 2020. Honeywell’s 2023 survey of workers in large buildings revealed 93% of respondents said their expectations for workplace air quality were higher than they were three years earlier.

But when I looked at survey data about the salience of air quality, I could barely find any evidence that COVID-19 — which was basically an indoor-transmission problem3 — had happened.

Since 2000, with a brief blip in 2005, Gallup has been asking Americans how much they personally worry about a variety of environmental problems, including water pollution, animal extinction, tropical rainforest survival, and air pollution. Air pollution, despite being the best-documented direct harm to humans, has basically always lagged the other concerns, but I was surprised how little the global pandemic seems to have affected views.

In 2019, 43% of Americans expressed a great deal of concern about air pollution, which went up to 48% in 2020 and then dropped to 41% in 2021 (which is exactly when we all figured out how important indoor transmission was!). By 2023, concern about air pollution was down to 38%.

Now, a virus isn’t colloquially understood to be pollution — though the EPA explicitly includes viruses among “biological pollutants.” So, perhaps respondents would have answered differently if primed to understand the question as including viruses.

This all forces me to revisit my initial condescending attitude to our ancestors, who struggled to understand the root causes of the year without a summer. After all, modernity may have given us the ability to explain our world’s problems in exquisite detail, yet we remain surprisingly casual about addressing them.

Top stories this week, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

As we grow, I want to make sure you see everything we’re doing without flooding your inbox with dozens of emails. But for the real libs, you can get every post as it drops by opting into The Mag here.

Big week at The Argument — Jeremiah Johnson made his debut as our newest staff writer. In his opening bid, he discussed how the new film Obsession fits within the prestige horror genre. “Anxieties are increasingly not about horrible monsters or alien forces tearing society apart,” he writes of the past decade in horror film. “They’re about what we’re doing to ourselves.” Read on for the full analysis:

Meanwhile, Eli Richman corrected the record: No, 2.8 million Americans were not induced to scream and vomit from overuse of marijuana. Somehow, a single bad study from 2018 fooled The Washington Post and The New York Times, muddying the debate on the effects of legalization. Get the real scoop right here:

Finally, Kelsey Piper took on superstar public intellectual Jonathan Haidt, who is on a campaign to age-gate the internet. She worries that age verification will threaten free speech and thinks that we should consider more balanced measures. “It’s ironic that the writer who gained prominence with a strong case for free speech is now in denial about what his second act’s political project seeks to do,” she writes of Haidt.

Read on for the full take:

🌟Abundance Wins of the Week🌟

  • This week, San Francisco lowered its inclusionary-housing mandate from 15% of new units to 5%.4 An April memo by the city controller’s office had previously concluded that anything significantly higher than 0% could unduly slow housing construction, but hey, progress is progress.

  • San Diego’s regional planning agency applied California’s SB 79 — a new law that upzones transit-adjacent areas — to 17 additional bus stop locations, overruling city officials who had identified only four. Estimates say this will add capacity for around 100,000 more units.

  • The House Subcommittee on Energy advanced six nuclear energy permitting bills to the full Energy and Commerce Committee. These bills would focus regulatory efforts, cut down the number of hearings required for nuclear projects, and more.

Worth watching...

I sometimes wonder how many times Sen. Bernie Sanders has said the word “billionaire” in the past decade. Through sheer repetition, he has almost single-handedly popularized the notion that we live in an “oligarchy,” and recently, he’s been stumping with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on a Fighting Oligarchy tour. But do we actually live in an oligarchy?

While billionaires don’t literally coordinate to get their way, they do have tremendous influence as a class. This week, Jerusalem and Matt clash over this question. Watch them untangle the debate below:

Kristen Soltis Anderson is one of the top right-of-center pollsters in the country and an expert in the youth vote. This week, she was a special guest on a Substack live conversation with our director of political data Lakshya Jain. Alongside VoteHub’s Zachary Donnini, they try to explain why the youth vote has swung so wildly in the past several election cycles.

Are zoomers becoming Democrats again? Or just doomers? Click below to find out:

What’s News with The Argument

The Argument recommends, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

Jeremiah Johnson, The Argument’s new staff writer, has decided to plant a flag. He is dedicating his first appearance in this section to a single bold assertion: Carly Rae Jepsen’s E*MO*TION is the greatest pure pop album of the last 25 years. Apparently, even the bonus tracks, like “Cut to the Feeling,” are required listening.

I will be assessing his claims on my commute home, with one eyebrow raised.

Meanwhile, Eli Richman told me he “must have walked around the museum room for over an hour” when he saw Laurie Anderson’s Four Talks at the Hirshhorn last weekend (not because he was lost but because he was absorbed).

For more than two weeks in 2021, Anderson spent 10 hours a day painting this room in a full stream of consciousness — no sketches beforehand — filling it with COVID-era reflections, dark jokes, expressions of modern anxiety, and more. I’m sold, Eli.

After years of declining recommendations to watch Couples Therapy, Maibritt Henkel binged a whole season this week.

“It sounds banal, but it’s such a good reminder that finding the language to describe how you feel and why you feel that way is a universally difficult skill,” she said.

Some people eventually do find words for this task, but others capture it in a novel artistic form. Video producer Justin Zuckerman saw Dry Leaf on Friday, a three-hour Georgian film about a father searching for his daughter in a vast, picturesque landscape. The entire film is shot on a 2008 cell phone.

“I’m excited because it’s presenting a story in a challenging way that I haven’t seen in cinema before,” Justin told me before seeing the film. “Even the trailer suggests something intimate and alive.”5

Speaking of intimacy, I saw The Invite in theaters last weekend. The film is about a double date that eventually reveals unspoken dimensions of the participants’ sex lives and preferences. It would have been easy to play it all for laughs, defusing every embarrassed tension with a joke, but the script deftly managed the line between humor and seriousness. It left me laughing and thinking in quick succession.

Finally, as Ontario sends wildfire smoke to D.C., Jerusalem is jamming out to a much better Ontarian export: Alanis Morissette's Jagged Little Pill album, which can be surprisingly repurposed to rage at a continental atmospheric transport event.

1

There were potentially other contributing causes to this bizarre climatic event: other volcanic explosions and something called the Dalton Minimum, which was a "period of reduced sunspot activity that occurred between roughly 1790 and 1830" (notably this effect is very different from the incorrect contemporaneous theory that dark spots on the sun were literally blocking the light).

2

As measured by the World Health Organization.

3

HEPA air cleaners can remove up to 99.97% of infectious aerosolized SARS-CoV-2. Mechanically ventilated classrooms had at least 74% lower student infection risk than those relying on natural ventilation.

4

With an exception for the Mission District — my once and future home neighborhood— where the limit is now 8%.

5

Justin Zuckerman has since reported that this is one of the best films he’s ever seen, and he went to film school. “It was like watching an impressionistic painting evolve live.”

item.title: The left’s climate denial problem
item.description: Fighting global warming is going to cost something
item.content:encoded:
By John Robert Thomason

The Argument is thrilled to announce that John Thomason is joining our growing editorial team as our senior editor.

John comes to us from Grist, the leading independent climate and environmental magazine, where he spent more than five years as the features editor on a team that won a 2023 National Magazine Award for general excellence. There, he commissioned long-form enterprise stories and argument-driven analysis, led much of the publication’s news coverage, and edited features recognized by a Sidney Award, a Murrow Award, and inclusion in The Best American Science and Nature Writing anthology, among other honors. Before joining Grist, he ran the fact-checking desk at The Intercept.

At The Argument, John will commission and edit essays, reported features, and cultural commentary; guide writers in sharpening their arguments; and write a regular column of his own. He will help set our editorial priorities, expand our contributor network, and mentor our junior staff and fellows, carrying forward the standard that defines us: sharp, rigorous arguments that confront the illiberal drift in our politics.

To support The Argument’s mission of revitalizing liberalism through public, rigorous debate, please consider becoming a paying subscriber. It’s how we bring on talented new writers, commission original polling, and produce fantastic audio and video content.

Join us. We’re Libbing Out.

Subscribe now

- Jerusalem Demsas, editor-in-chief

Climate policy is trade-offs all the way down. That’s because we’re trying to balance the harms of global warming with the benefits of modern energy and industry. If the only thing we wanted to do was eliminate carbon emissions, we would find a giant “off” button for the global economy and press it as fast as possible.

The closest we’ve come to realizing this hypothetical was in the spring of 2020. Daily global emissions plummeted by more than 15%, compared with average 2019 levels, as the nascent COVID-19 pandemic shut down large swaths of commerce, travel, and education. Ultimately, nobody thought this trade-off — which involved unemployment, learning loss, and delayed or forgone health care — was worth the dip in pollution, so nobody has seriously proposed hitting the “off” switch again.

Share

What the COVID experience revealed is that, whether environmentalists admit it or not, every climate policy implicitly involves what’s called a cost-benefit analysis — an effort to tally up all the gains and losses of a potential policy and figure out which sum is larger.

Cost-benefit analysis gets a bad rap among progressives because the Reagan administration made a big show of mandating the procedure for major new regulatory actions. But that doesn’t mean cost-benefit analysis is necessarily a right-wing framework; it’s all about how you use it. One could just as easily use the method as a check on the deregulatory zeal of a conservative administration.

The principles of cost-benefit analysis are useful for those of us who are climate-concerned because they force us to ask, as a very first step: Are our actions likely to reduce carbon emissions, relative to the counterfactual?

As obvious as that sounds, this interrogation happens less often than you might think.

Consider Obama’s cancellation of the Keystone XL pipeline, which environmentalists heralded as one of the defining climate wins of the 2010s. This is despite the fact that Obama’s own State Department, headed by noted climate hawk John Kerry, found that killing the pipeline would not lead to a reduction in global carbon emissions. That’s because the Canadian tar sands oil in question would still reach the global market by rail. (In fact, emissions associated with transporting the oil might well increase in this scenario, as would the risk of spills given the very real possibility of train derailments.)

While subsequent academic research has challenged the State Department’s claim — it projects some global demand destruction due to higher prices commanded by oil without the pipeline — even these researchers admit that there is no way to know if blocking the pipeline reduced global emissions. Compare that unknown (at best) emissions benefit to the millions and millions of philanthropic dollars expended — not to mention the countless hours devoted by smart, committed activists — on the campaign to block Keystone.

Subscribe now

Even actions that do clearly reduce emissions can benefit from the context of a cost-benefit analysis. One of the primary policies that U.S. states have used to decarbonize electricity generation is so-called renewable portfolio standards, or RPS. These standards require that a certain portion of states’ energy needs be met with renewable resources like wind and solar — in other words, that emissions-intensive forms of energy are directly substituted with carbon-free alternatives.

The good news is that the most comprehensive academic research on RPS found that the policies worked: States that instituted the standards saw an 11% to 24% drop in emissions after seven years and a 25% to 41% drop after 12.

But to figure out whether this was worth the cost, you have to first do some other math to figure out how costly those carbon emissions actually are. And that’s the really hard part.

All disagreements about climate policy are disagreements about the relative balance of costs and benefits

Because costs and benefits come in many different forms — when it comes to climate change, the costs alone might involve lives lost, labor forgone, damaged infrastructure, ecosystem destruction, and much more — the standard approach is to convert everything into dollar costs that can be measured against each other. Beginning during the Obama administration, all of these harms got tallied together into one big number called the social cost of carbon (SCC).

A larger SCC will counsel larger and more dramatic interventions, so a lot rides on just how big you think the costs of climate change are.

Obama set this number at $43 per ton, and when Donald Trump took office, his administration dropped the number to under $10. Biden then proposed bumping the figure up to nearly $200. (Last year, Trump ditched the metric entirely.)

Think about the multiples involved here. The Biden administration’s claim was that the first Trump administration was underestimating the harms of climate change by a factor of at least 20, and it planned to make changes across federal policy to account for that.

Suppose the Environmental Protection Agency was considering a regulation that would cost businesses and consumers $1 billion but prevent 10 million tons of carbon emissions — the equivalent of well over 1 million U.S. homes’ annual energy use. Under the first Trump administration, the rule would produce at most only $100 million in climate benefits and therefore fail the cost-benefit test. Under the Obama-era estimate, it would produce $430 million in climate benefits but still fail.

Under the Biden administration, however, it would produce $1.9 billion in benefits and would therefore be justified.

Now we can look back at the apparently successful renewable portfolio standards — the state-level rules that led to big drops in emissions — and see how they fared under these frameworks. The cost per ton of emissions avoided was $86 to $211, which exceeds the Obama administration’s SCC (and perhaps even Biden’s) and is much higher than abatement costs of other policies proven to reduce power sector emissions, like the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, a carbon pricing framework that many Northeast and mid-Atlantic states participate in.

This suggests that, at worst, RPS policies may have caused more harm than they produced in climate benefits. And, at best, they were probably a worse use of resources than alternatives like cap and trade.

Climate advocates sometimes chafe at this sort of analysis when it cautions against their side’s policy aims, but they implicitly buy into it all the time. For instance, Greenpeace called the Green New Deal a “bargain” because of the estimated $500 billion in annual climate damages the organization suggested the policy would prevent. Climate Power published an entire report arguing that climate change “could cost the U.S. economy $14.5 trillion and result in a loss of 900,000 jobs annually by 2070.” And it’s a staple of climate journalism to explain new projections of the economic cost of climate change.

If you’re going to sound the alarm about a future decline in GDP, you can’t justify ignoring the way the very remedies you’re proposing entail GDP losses in the present. But this is standard in environmentalist discourse.

Subscribe now

John Kerry’s State Department estimated that completing Keystone XL would contribute $3.4 billion to the U.S. GDP. That doesn’t necessarily mean it was worth it, but it is a fact that is worth considering in the “costs” column — and comparing to the campaign’s negligible and uncertain benefits.

Luckily, there are plenty of ways to reduce emissions that also happen to be economically efficient — where it’s the cost side of the ledger that is negligible, rather than the benefits. In fact, there are so many options here that you can really let your personal passions guide your final choice.

Mad about bipartisan Sinophobia and distressed about saber-rattling toward China? You could campaign to legalize imports of the world’s cheapest electric cars. Are you an urbanist who hates personal car ownership? Why not ask your city council to welcome all-electric Waymos?

If you’re disgusted with the fossil fuel industry, you could electrify your home. If you agree with Bill McKibben that it’s time for environmentalists to get out of the way of new clean energy projects, you could call your representatives and ask them to support federal permitting reform.

But while it’s true that many of these avenues could reduce emissions while contributing to overall economic growth, it’s not quite true to say that they don’t have costs. Cheap electric cars will disadvantage U.S.-based automakers. Waymos will put taxi and Uber drivers out of work and cut into the business of car dealerships. And permitting reform will erode the veto power of U.S. landowners.

I personally think these are costs worth bearing for the future benefit of all of humanity. An open question, however, is whether or not liberals think any interest groups are worth disadvantaging in pursuit of climate victories that are real rather than symbolic.

Have you heard the good news about global warming?

Two fundamental facts about climate change counsel against despair. The first is that the problem is global in the deepest sense: The climate does not care where emissions come from. One ton of atmospheric carbon emitted in Alberta has the same effect as a ton emitted in Jakarta, which has the same effect as a ton emitted in Dubai.

As a large, rich country that uses a lot of energy, U.S. emissions matter a great deal — but they won’t come even close to being the primary determinant of the world’s climate trajectory from this point on. (And on the global front, recent years have brought quite a bit of hope as renewable energy begins to crowd out fossil fuels.)

The second relevant fact is that the problem is fundamentally incremental. What matters for global warming is the total volume of carbon that accumulates in the atmosphere. More carbon is worse, and less is better.

The same logic applies to global average temperature: Just as 2 degrees Celsius of warming is “better” than 2.1 degrees, 2.1 is better than 2.5, and 2.5 is better than 3. And because the impacts of climate change don’t scale linearly with warming, each tenth or hundredth or thousandth of a degree avoided is a big, big win.

There are no thresholds we need to avoid. We just need to eliminate as many emissions as possible.

Everyone who’s spent any amount of time on the issue knows these facts, but following their implications entails a dramatically different approach to climate activism than what dominates today. Long-shot efforts at systemic change — be it to abolish the fossil fuel industry or capitalism itself — do not present a clear path to reducing emissions. By far the most useful thing you can do as a climate-concerned citizen is push for the most efficient emissions reductions possible in whatever sphere you can influence.

But when it comes to climate change, “most efficient” is a tall order. So don’t get too hung up on every single number in the cost-benefit ledger. If you are reasonably confident that 1) emissions will actually go down and 2) the social costs are negligible, then get to work.

item.title: Bernie’s bad bet on OpenAI
item.description: Nationalizing AI labs won’t support the welfare state
item.content:encoded:
By Kobe Yank-Jacobs

Right now, the financial future of American labs like OpenAI and Anthropic is built upon their ability to charge a premium for their services. Elected officials like Sen. Bernie Sanders are also counting on the dominance of these Big Tech companies to fund massive expansions of the welfare state. Open models could destroy both OpenAI’s current business model and the case for nationalizing AI labs.

Last week, one Chinese company struck a blow to both of those dreams: Moonshot released an open model that is near the frontier of AI capability: Kimi K3.1

In contrast to proprietary models like Claude and ChatGPT, an open model is one that can be downloaded from the internet and customized without a pricey subscription or annoying usage cap.2

Just like most businesses don’t need the smartest guy from Harvard Law to run their legal department, most businesses don’t need the frontier capabilities promised by leading proprietary models. They just need 90th-percentile versions they can adjust to fit their particular needs.

In June, Sanders proposed that the federal government take a 50% equity stake in the biggest labs in order to seed a public wealth fund, the idea being that the fund would redistribute income to counteract the economic fallout of AI. Sam Altman floated the same idea to the administration — he’s proposed a smaller 5% stake — and Donald Trump mused aloud about it on Air Force One. Early polling suggests strong public support for these schemes.

But there is simply no guarantee that the businesses currently at the technological and financial frontier of the AI boom will be the ones to capture its largest upsides. That distinction — between creating value and capturing it — is one of the oldest problems in the economics of innovation. Modern history is full of technological breakthroughs where the benefits wound up accumulating in unexpected places.

An influential 2004 paper by economist William Nordhaus argued that for every dollar of social value innovators create, they capture only about 2 cents. Nordhaus suggested that the dot-com bubble arose because investors believed that just because the internet had enormous social value, particular internet companies would be great bets. Yahoo, valued at roughly $125 billion in 2000, was ultimately sold for just $4.48 billion in 2017.

Policymakers should have a high degree of uncertainty about where we think most of AI’s value will accrue — and they should design tax policies that don’t assume all the tax revenue should come from a couple of leading modern labs.

In other words, whatever policies exist to distribute the gains of AI wealth should be agnostic to who exactly wins out in the marketplace. When the dust settles, old-school progressive tax reform — raising corporate taxes, closing loopholes, making sure CEOs pay higher taxes than their secretaries — will capture more value across the whole economy than policies like selective public ownership, since those are narrowly targeted at present-day incumbents.

We are in the very early days of figuring out how AI gets monetized. OpenAI and Anthropic may have valuations approaching $1 trillion, but that doesn’t mean their investors have taken all the right bets — and it doesn’t mean the American public should be taking the same ones.

Open models rush in

Earlier in the AI race, open models tended to be six to 10 months behind the frontier, but newer models like Kimi K3 now seem to be achieving top-tier capability only about three or four months after the leading models. The more this gap closes, the more the free models will be considered good enough for most use cases.

Even if the capability gap stays where it is, the market effect may be the same. In addition to Moonshot, the Chinese company Alibaba has previewed an equally competitive version of its open model, Qwen, while Z.ai’s top model already outcompetes all of Google’s proprietary models (though not OpenAI’s or Anthropic’s).

Meanwhile, more American companies are getting in the game, too, even if they lag behind Chinese open models on capability.

Last week, Thinking Machines Lab (founded by Mira Murati, formerly the CTO at OpenAI) released its first open model. Reflection, a company dedicated to open models, has touted a first release coming later this year. And Nvidia, the famous chipmaker, has both released its own open models and convened a large coalition of companies, including the French lab Mistral, to create more.

In other words, downward pricing pressure on the leading labs can come from more comparable models or just a flood of new entrants.

Of course, these open model providers are businesses, too; they are giving away the model so they can monetize other parts of the AI ecosystem. Maybe that’s infrastructure (chips in Nvidia’s case) or perhaps the service of helping an end user tailor the model (Reflection’s likely approach). In other words, the “AI market” is not one thing — it’s a stack of infrastructural and software elements.

To understand which part of that stack open models threaten, consider what happens each time you ask ChatGPT a question: OpenAI takes care of what’s called “inference,” or the actual computation of your prompt and its response. OpenAI may not own the chips that help with this. But it guarantees that its top-tier model will be available for you so you don’t have to find the chip capacity yourself.

This is likely a large part of what drives your subscription pricing, and it’s why more complex AI use cases are billed by usage. Each request costs more inference.

With open models, businesses can shop for the lowest inference price through third-party providers, and they also aren’t paying the markup for accessing state-of-the-art models themselves.3

It’s not like the big labs don’t know all this. It’s not like their investors are ignorant. The question is how they are planning to capture value and justify their massive valuations regardless.

Competition around every corner

Once multiple labs can make models that are all good enough, customers will stop caring so much about which one they use and will instead compare mostly on things like price. Arvind Narayanan, one of the influential authors of the blog AI as Normal Technology, and Akash Kapur, a visiting fellow at Princeton, argued that once this happens, firms can either become more like software companies or more like infrastructure businesses.

The trouble with infrastructure is that it tends to be hard to differentiate the core product. Electricity is the same regardless of which company generates the electrons. That makes it difficult to sustain unusually high margins unless companies can create some other source of differentiation or market power (which electric utilities have because they are regulated monopolies).

So Narayanan and Kapur concluded that, historically, capital-intensive industries have avoided becoming interchangeable when they make it difficult for customers to switch away from their products. (Imagine switching your company from Slack to Teams. It’s doable, but it’s a hassle.)

For this reason, they argued that, to become profitable, AI labs need to move “up the stack” rather than down it, toward software rather than infrastructure. The labs need to try to lock their large consumer bases into their software platforms through more valuable software services, they said. This could look like Anthropic or OpenAI creating and licensing digital remote workers or specializing in helping companies redesign their workflows around the product.

For our purposes, it’s enough to say that anywhere they turn — up or down the stack — the major labs face significant competition. Even in this seemingly preferable “up the stack” scenario, Anthropic and OpenAI face incumbents like Google and Microsoft, while turning down the stack subjects them to the low-margin trench warfare like that waged in the telecom and airline businesses.

The labs may still figure out how to hold a winning place in the market and justify their valuations — but even that is not the same as being the primary winners of an unprecedented windfall by controlling the top-tier version of a transformative technology.

Creating value isn’t the same thing as capturing it

Even if OpenAI ends up becoming enormously valuable, its profits may still end up being small relative to the amount of growth AI produces across the rest of the economy.

Railroads are the best example. Yes, the firms that built railroads made a bunch of money off passengers and firms using their infrastructure, but that profit paled in comparison to what it did to land values near train stations. Removing the entire 1890 railroad network would have reduced the value of U.S. agricultural land by 60% — landowners, not railroad companies, captured the majority of the benefit.

Electricity showed the same pattern. Almost every business in the modern world uses electricity, from the deli running its meat slicer to the chemical plant running complex industrial processes. But in those cases, most of the value is going to the business that uses electricity, not to the generator or the distributor.

While the early electricity industry did generate a few moguls, in the long run, owning a utility was not the way to the top. The emblematic fortune of the electrical age was not the utility owner; it was Henry Ford, whose factories used electric power to produce a more valuable downstream product.

As Narayanan and Kapur pointed out, the same thing applied to telecom and fiber. “During the telecom and fiber buildout of the late 1990s, capacity exploded 186,000-fold in seven years, prices crashed, and roughly $2 trillion in market capitalization was erased,” they wrote. “The value generated by the infrastructure primarily accrued to industries and applications built on top of it.”

While telecom had its boom, the trick was to be Jeff Bezos, building an internet company that put instantaneous global communication to good use. And the original dot-com boom itself saw this same dynamic.

The IBM PC is an even closer analogy to open models. To get to market quickly, IBM used off-the-shelf components, licensed Microsoft’s operating system, chose an Intel processor, and published technical specifications. The open architecture made the IBM PC the industry standard — and allowed competitors to clone it. Its PC market share fell from roughly 80% in the early 1980s to 20% a decade later, while firms like Microsoft and Intel reaped most of the profits.

So, in the present context, trying to fund a massive public policy through taxes on the AI labs themselves amounts to a nested bet: first, that AI actually does produce returns at some unprecedented rate, second, that the labs themselves are the ones to capture that wealth, and third, that the particular layer occupied by today’s labs remains scarce and defensible rather than becoming a low-margin input that shifts profits somewhere else.

The old tax solutions are the new tax solutions

All of this is why a narrow tax or equity stake on a few notable model developers is a very bad way to go about redistributing the wealth gains from AI.

The wealth from AI will be in the pockets of people whose business may have nothing to do with models, chips, or clouds. It may accrue to lawyers who become able to serve three times as many clients as they did before AI, a manufacturer whose widgets leave the line twice as fast, or a landowner whose property becomes more productive and valuable.

In fact, the more economically transformative AI is, the more it follows that value is going to spread to non-AI businesses. The wealth of any boom goes to those who capture productivity gains and invent novel products. AI will make the capital class as a whole more wealthy. And if that’s the case, we need a funding mechanism that captures all this wealth.

The point is not that model labs can’t become huge and durable companies — some pioneers do build moats — the point is that the magnitude of a technology’s social value tells us remarkably little about how much of that value any one pioneer will capture.

An idea like taking an equity stake in the labs could produce a lot of money, but that’s a risky bet when a broad-based tax hike is sure to produce a lot of money.

In a recent The New York Times op-ed about the equity stake proposal, the Council on Foreign Relations’ Sebastian Mallaby put some figures on an optimistic scenario (assuming Altman’s 5% figure wins out over Sanders’ 50%). He calculated that even if the major labs’ shares rise at 20% per year — about double the S&P 500’s average over the past two decades — the public wealth fund would yield under $30,000 per U.S. citizen after 10 years.

For context, that’s only a quarter of the per-capita value of Alaska’s sovereign wealth fund (which is supported by the state’s oil revenue). And that fund only pays out $1,000 per year.

This is not remotely close to a basic income. It’s at best a small buffer against a turbulent economy.

Any proposal that takes the possibility of massive job losses seriously has to look more broadly at the issue. It has to be premised on the notion that we can’t predict where gains will accrue, that the value from a general-purpose technology does not always show up as income connected to the technology itself. It will show up across the economy. In the case of a labor-displacing technology, it could show up mostly as returns to capital.

AI growth requires getting ready for a world where we don’t — and can’t — know who will get rich off it. The tax base has to follow the gains wherever they appear, not bet the welfare state on owning today’s top performer.

Subscribe now

Recommended reading:

1

Measures of capability like Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index or Epoch AI’s Epoch Capabilities Index aggregate and weight across a number of benchmarks. What this means is that individual models that appear close to each other in the index might be better or worse on some given task type — so if Kimi K3 lags GPT 5.6 overall, it may still do better at, say, math problems.

On top of that, since open models can be further tuned by their users, an open model can be trained to improve in a specific domain such that it is indistinguishable from “frontier” intelligence on that task (a point open model expert Nathan Lambert raised in his recent podcast).

2

There is a distinction between open-source and open-weights models. Open source means that the training data and the code are released in addition to the model weights, while open weights only releases the model weights. In this piece, open model refers to the latter, which is what most labs mentioned here are doing.

Importantly, Moonshot is releasing its weights on July 27, almost two weeks after the initial model release.

3

The prices of inference have been collapsing over the past 18 months — that is something you would expect from this kind of open model competition, but it also has many causes, and the trend preexisted open model progress.

item.title: The right can't handle complicated men
item.description: Welcome to the summer of Homer
item.content:encoded:
By Maibritt Henkel

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Maibritt Henkel

Years before taking aim at Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of The Odyssey, the online right tried to cancel the 2017 translation of Homer that inspired him.

Far-right personalities like Bronze Age Pervert and his disciples have declared the translator, University of Pennsylvania professor Emily Wilson, a woke phony on a mission to emasculate Homer. They see a vindictive feminist — the first woman to complete a major English transla1tion of the poem — who holds all things white, male, and Western in contempt and, like Nolan’s multiracial cast, has sullied a precious urtext of the white, male, Western canon.

“Emily Wilson’s translation of the Odyssey sucks because she associates a belittling word with Odysseus wherever she can,” reads one tweet from Roman Helmet Guy. The account Raw Egg Nationalist posted a picture of a heavily tattooed Wilson next to the caption: “Women who look like this have no interest in anything other than revenging themselves on the men who have failed them.”

But the right’s critiques of Wilson’s translation do not reflect a close reading of her text — or a sophisticated understanding of Homer. In fact, Wilson’s decisions to render Odysseus “complicated”, omit sexist slurs, and favor unvarnished narrative over rhetorical flourish promote an accurate and traditional understanding of the poem, rather than undermine it. To call this “woke” is to expose how arbitrary that epithet has become — and how uninterested those who wield it are in good-faith debate, let alone the ancient Greeks they claim to celebrate.

Yes, Odysseus was complicated

According to some critics, Wilson’s hateful woke-ification of The Odyssey begins with her translation of the poem’s very first line. Where her predecessors have taken the Greek adjective “polytropos” to mean “the various-minded man” or “the man of twists and turns,” Wilson opts for “a complicated man.”

To anyone already convinced that Wilson has no respect for Homer, antiquity, or the discipline of translation, the word “complicated” represents a tedious progressive slight. The left doesn’t want you to celebrate Greek heroes just as it doesn’t want you to celebrate Columbus Day or Confederate monuments. For left-wing scolds, every glorious victory must be followed by an “it’s complicated.”

There are two problems here. The first is that “complicated” is not an inherently negative descriptor. The translation does not begin with the line “Tell me a story about a sexist piece of trash.”

As Wilson writes on her own Substack: “To me, ‘complicated’ doesn’t suggest either ‘good guy’ or ‘bad guy’: it’s a promise that this poem doesn’t stoop to those implausible simplifications.”

Then there’s the fact that Odysseus’ track record really is complicated. He owns slaves, pillages villages, brutally mutilates his enemies, and repeatedly cheats on his wife. Any self-respecting cancel culture would dismiss him in a second. But this is not Wilson’s approach. Her translation makes the case that Odysseus, despite all the sexism and slavery, is still a character who can speak to all of us. Much more than her critics do, Wilson is trying to defend his enduring relevance to modern readers — and that of the text as a whole.

Comparing her version to previous translations only underscores this point.

An essay in the Claremont Review of Books, the highbrow Trumpist journal, advises teachers against Wilson’s translations citing her “hostility to manly bravado.” A worthy translation must instead “honor Homer and his champions for who they are.” The essay instead recommends Fagles and Lattimore to those seeking to read Homer in English. And sure enough, there are several scenes in Fagles’ Odyssey that read quite differently from Wilson’s.

Take, for instance, the infamous scene in The Odyssey —tactfully left out by Nolan in the new adaptation — in which Odysseus’ son, Telemachus, has 12 female slaves killed for sleeping with Penelope’s suitors.

This is how Fagles translates the order given by Telemachus:

“No clean death for the likes of them, by god!

Not from me — they showered abuse on my head,

My mother’s too!

You sluts — the suitors’ whores!”

Emily Wilson’s translation reads as follows:

“I refuse to grant these girls

A clean death, since they poured down shame on me

And Mother, when they lay beside the suitors.”

That Wilson’s Telemachus does not call the girls “sluts” or “whores” is easy to mistake for some kind of modern feminist statement. In fact, her omission is truer to the original Greek, which does not feature any slur or epithet in the scene.

Fagles is often held up by Wilson’s critics as the more faithful, intellectually rigorous translator—the one serious people interested only in the unadulterated words of Homer should read. But in this passage, it is Fagles, not Wilson, who takes the liberty of giving Homer a moralizing twist.

This example also exposes how arbitrary the logic of what is and is not woke has become. Imagine if Wilson had been the one to add the modern pejoratives instead of Fagles. Wouldn’t that be more consistent with the notion that she is a man-hating lib, looking for any excuse to frame male characters as misogynistic bastards?

And, of course, anyone concerned about Wilson’s secret feminist agenda could simply listen to what she herself has said on the matter: “I keep urging journalists to ask men about their gender and how it informs their work, and please stop asking me about it, because I really don’t work on gender and it’s not my main interest.”

Subscribe now

Twitter trolls don’t care about iambic pentameter

Gender politics aside, there is a technical explanation for why Emily Wilson’s edition can be considered more faithful to the shape of the original poem than the 60-some translations that came before it.

Wilson is the first English translator to confine herself to exactly the same number of lines as the original Greek. She also opted to write the entire poem in iambic pentameter, rather than free verse or prose, honoring the regular verse form of the poem.2

To pull this off, she had to keep her sentences more direct and less ornate than her predecessors. As a result, Wilson’s translation is unusually concise.

That Wilson’s Odyssey has less sentimental flair and pomp than earlier translations doesn’t make it a hateful indictment of Odysseus. Her translation is not a progressive manifesto that delights in the downfall of men. Nor is it a contrived celebration of comic-book-style heroism. Instead it is a tight, technically accurate translation of a 2,700-year-old-poem that turns out to be a lot more morally ambiguous than many modern readers can handle.

Top stories this week, by Milan Singh

As we grow, I want to make sure you see everything we’re doing without flooding your inbox with dozens of emails. But for the real libs, you can get every post as it drops by opting into The Mag here.

Another week, another new hire at The Argument. We’re excited to welcome John Thomason as our new senior editor. In his first piece, he discussed the climate left’s inability to set priorities. Fighting climate change is costly — both politically and economically — and some battles, such as the fight over Keystone XL pipeline, just might not be worth the squeeze.

Kelsey Piper wrote about the controversy surrounding elite public high schools such as Stuyvesant in New York City. These schools admit very few Black and Hispanic students, but that’s not because their entrance exams are racist; it’s because the exams reveal underlying inequality. But as Kelsey notes, many more Black students gained admission to New York City’s competitive schools in the 1970s, read below to find out what changed.

Both Bernie Sanders and Sam Altman have proposed giving the government an equity stake in the major AI labs. But staking the future of the welfare state on the profitability of OpenAI and Anthropic is a risky bet, Kobe Yank-Jacobs argues. The labs that develop cutting-edge large language models won’t necessarily be the ones that reap the profits from their innovations. Instead, we should go back to the basics and focus on raising taxes on capital.

🌟Abundance Wins of the Week🌟

  • Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced new reforms to simplify permitting and cut fines and fees for small businesses in New York City.

  • The Portland Planning Commission in Oregon unanimously recommended that the City Council adopt several YIMBY reforms to the city’s zoning code, as required by state law.

  • $1.7 billion solar project broke ground in Texas underscoring the Lone Star State’s dominance in utility-scale solar generation.

Share

Worth watching...

This week on the podcast, Matt and Jerusalem were joined by Tim Lee, author of the newsletter Understanding AI, to discuss whether AI will automate everyone’s jobs. Jerusalem and Tim are optimistic; Matt thinks that the doomers are right to be worried. Give it a listen and decide for yourself!

What’s News with The Argument

The Argument recommends, by Milan Singh

This week, we decided to all stay on theme and recommend all things Odyssey-related:

Jerusalem recommended the oil painting Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses by John William Waterhouse: “It depicts Circe offering a potion to Odysseus, whose wary expression is captured in the mirror behind the witch. I just love everything about this painting Circe in the center of this image, one of Odysseus’ men-as-pig at her feet, and our hero relegated to a small reflection. It manages to make you feel entranced by the witch, just as she desires.”

Jeremiah Johnson gave honorable mentions to the movie O Brother Where Art Thou — one of his “favorite movies ever” — as well as the book Circe, a recommendation seconded by several others in the office (except for Jerusalem, who said she couldn’t get through it).

Maibritt recommended The Song of Achilles, which her grandmother gave her. It’s one of her favorite books of all time, and she told me that she probably rereads it once a year. “If you also felt that Nolan’s Odyssey was a little short on homoeroticism, this is the book for you.”

Finally, Angela said that she “could not recommend enough” the 2004 film The SpongeBob SquarePants Movie, which is “basically a 1:1” retelling of The Odyssey , featuring:

  • SpongeBob and Patrick leaving home to go on a quest

  • Poseidon, Princess Mindy as Athena, and David Hasselhoff as the divine intermediary

  • A magical bag of winds

  • A scuba diver standing in for Polyphemus

  • Plankton playing the role of the suitors and trying to take over the Krusty Krab

  • The old lady with the ice cream as a parallel to Circe.

Personally, I think that’s the best take I’ve heard during the entire time I’ve been working here.

1

Scholar Anne Dacier translated the Odyssey into French in 1716.

2

While most recent translations of The Odyssey do not adhere to a strict metrical pattern, Wilson wanted to recreate the rhythmic experience of the original text. In Greek, the poem uses dactylic hexameter, the standard verse form of archaic poetry. In her modern translation, Wilson opts for iambic pentameter because it is the most common meter in dramatic English verse. Every line contains 10 syllables, broken into five pairs of alternating unstressed (da) and stressed (DUM) beats.

item.title: In defense of gerontocracy
item.content:encoded:
By Matthew Yglesias

In today’s hyperpolarized, hyperfactionalized political climate, one of the most reliable ways to get hosannas from every corner of the internet is to fulminate against the tyranny of America’s elderly.

Case in point: Last week, a reporter for the San Francisco Chronicle tweeted out a photo of a local town hall where residents were gathered to discuss a proposed set of new housing developments.

As one would expect, the audience members were… grayer than the average San Franciscan.

This spurred some normie YIMBY arguments about how community meetings are unrepresentative venues for political debate, as well as some ruder commentary about how old people suck and we should get rid of them.

The implication is that we live in a gerontocracy — a society where American seniors are not only clogging community meetings with their unreasonable opposition to new development but also hoarding power and opportunity in every profession and at the highest levels of government.

There are, of course, some valid concerns about the fiscal consequences of population aging and some very real cases of elected officials who have overstayed their welcome. It’s also just true that, from the C-suite to the legal profession to academia, there are more old people hanging on longer than ever.

It’s hard not to sympathize with ambitious young elected officials tired of waiting for plum congressional seats to open up or academics angry that it’s so hard to get on the tenure track these days. But it’s worth reflecting that the primary reason you see older people hanging on to prominent roles these days is entirely benign — Americans are living longer.

Share

This fact is broadly known, but I think the specific dynamics are a bit misunderstood and underrated. A recent working paper by Liran Einav and Amy Finkelstein, for example, looked at nearly three decades of data from the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey and reached the conclusion that, while declining mortality and morbidity has increased Social Security costs by 14% per beneficiary, it has only driven up per-beneficiary Medicare costs by a much more modest 6%.

Why the mismatch between the two programs? Well, it’s because people aren’t just living longer; they are living better. The authors wrote that the increase in expected lifespan since 1992 has featured additional years that “were entirely healthy — free of physical or cognitive limitations — while the expected amount of time spent with severe health limitations fell by about 30%, reducing expected lifetime nursing-home and home-health use.”

That’s boring accounting stuff, far removed from the fun of hot takes about elderly opportunity hoarding. But it’s very relevant to how we ought to understand the gerontocracy problem. If people are living not only longer, but specifically longer in good health, then of course they are going to linger longer in leadership positions.

And, of course, not all of those people will retain their mental faculties or know when to call it.

Five members of the House of Representatives and one U.S. Senator have died in office this Congress with many cases involving members who had been ill or infirm for a while and missed the opportunity to stand down in a timely manner.

That said, congressional deaths are not exactly a new phenomenon. There was a run of about 50 years before the Civil War in which at least five members died in office in every single Congress. Congress was also much smaller back then, so the mortality rate was consistently a lot higher than in the present Congress. Further, dying members were younger, on average, than today’s dying members — but that’s because people died much younger 200 years ago.

Congressional mortality reached its peak in the 1930s and 1940s when you would routinely have over 20 members dying in a single Congress. As Slate’s Ian Prasad Philbrick wrote in April, the past few Congresses have seen a genuine uptick in deaths. But that’s because the 2010s had unusually low death rates, not because the 2020s have had unusually many.

Of course, death is a crude measure of impairment. But paired with the finding that, population-wide, people are living more unimpaired years, the fact that the congressional death rate is lower than normal, not higher, should give us some confidence that things are OK on average.

Subscribe now

Similarly, the fact that the “gerontocracy” trend isn’t limited to politics or academia but includes corporate America ought to be viewed as reassuring.

The business world is quite ruthless and competitive. Changes in corporate legal structure over the past 40 to 50 years have only made it more cutthroat. An executive team that doesn’t deliver shareholder value is liable to get fired by the board of directors. If inertia, office politics, and the old boys’ club prevent that from happening, these days, there are any number of activist equity funds eager to sweep in, buy up companies with depressed share prices, and make changes.

Nobody should be utopian about the efficiency of real-world markets, but unless you believe American finance has become cuddlier over the past generation, you ought to acknowledge that we have less reason than ever to think that for-profit companies are irrationally coddling the elderly. We have more old managers than before because it makes business sense, which is a reassuring signal about parallel trends in other fields.

Or consider the medical evidence on dementia. Due to rising life expectancy and lack of good treatments, widespread dementia is a problem that is very much still with us. But dementia rates are falling at all ages. People in their early 90s today appear to have sharper mental acuity than people who were 10 years younger in the 1980s.

If “gerontocracy” just means that a higher proportion of people live into their 70s while being in much better mental and physical shape than the septuagenarians of the past, then what is there to complain about?

We should complain about real problems

Well, of course there is plenty to complain about in life. Renters, disproportionately young, have taken it on the chin due to America’s accelerating housing shortage. By the same token (and for essentially the same reason), it has become harder for young people to buy homes.

These are real problems, and you can lay them at the feet of the elderly in the sense that the relevant policies were mostly put in place in the 1970s and the 1980s when today’s old people were around and today’s young people weren’t. But if you look at the various state-level YIMBY success stories in recent years, it’s not as if they were achieved by somehow disempowering old people.

Indeed, America’s oldest state, Maine, passed sweeping housing measures last year that have the state now exceeding its annual housing production goals. The second-oldest state, New Hampshire, also passed sweeping reforms.

But, of course, the battle for housing abundance is not yet won. People have widespread erroneous opinions about the relevant economic issues, and there is widespread irrational dislike of developers. Trying to tackle these problems directly with better arguments, new cultural products, and political organizing seems a lot more fruitful than complaining about gerontocracy and needlessly antagonizing old people.

Share

Now, it’s true that if we ameliorate the housing shortage, we will likely see people forming new households and new families at younger ages. This will lead to at least somewhat more children being born and alter the demographic trajectory of the country in a more youthful direction. But that’s to say that population aging is in part an effect of other bad policies, not that the existence of old people is bad.

Similarly, a very real problem in Congress is that the vast majority of members do not face competitive general elections. This allows infirm members to linger in office longer than they should. This is bad. But the badness is not unique to age. Democratic House nominee Darializa Avila Chevalier seems like a crazy person and is all but guaranteed to prevail in her general election due to the low levels of electoral competition, but she’s definitely young.

The tendency for political power to be controlled by low-turnout primaries, in other words, is worth fixing. It would address some legitimate concerns about “gerontocracy” while also addressing a bunch of legitimate concerns that have nothing whatsoever to do with age.

Meanwhile, though America’s frustrated young academics yearning for greater upward mobility cut a wide swath in the discourse thanks to their strong verbal skills and abundant free time, I’m not persuaded that this is a legitimate social problem. The fundamental reason that it’s hard to get a job as a historian is that there is not a lot of demand for the services of historians. This is aggravating for the specific people involved, but there are lots of fields where the number of people who would like to do the job exceeds the number of positions actually available. And there’s plenty of the opposite:

America really could use more good K-12 teachers. We could use more people with the kind of progressive values prevalent in academia working as police officers. We could use more research scientists.

For better or worse, in life, you need to find something to do that is useful to other people. Looking at declining demand for certain categories of academic work and pronouncing it gerontocracy is unhelpful.

The good news about the bad news

This all brings us back to the boring green eyeshades. The United States committed, some time ago, to meeting the financial and medical needs of its elderly population. As the older share of the total population has grown, this commitment has become increasingly burdensome.

That’s a genuine problem.

Russ Greene, a right-wing economic commentator and executive director at the Prime Mover Institute, coined the term “Total Boomer Luxury Communism“ to describe the mass redistribution of wealth from younger families and workers to the elderly. In many ways, his argument is similar to that found in Samuel Moyn’s recent book Gerontocracy in America. But as a right-wing rather than left-wing guy, he is willing to bite the bullet and say we need to cut entitlement spending.

But to a certain extent, the gerontocracy frame makes this harder rather than easier to solve.

Subscribe now

For starters, the simple fact of the matter is that the political durability of Social Security and Medicare is not a question of older people exerting raw electoral power.

These programs are broadly popular with all age groups in the electorate.

Both programs are seen as working well, with funds seen as going to largely worthy, sympathetic recipients.

Voters are also just fairly change-averse. If you proposed creating new programs on the scale of Social Security or Medicare, voters would be alarmed by the vast new spending. But these have existed for a long time and have grown slowly, so instead, the idea of cutting them alarms people.

Logically, though, if the problem is that people are living longer, then a big part of the solution should be to ask people to work longer.

I used to worry a lot about this idea because the prospect of compelling nice-but-frail old people into the labor market feels ghoulish. But understanding that “gerontocracy” is just downstream of the reality that people are living more years in perfectly good health changes the picture.

People are staying on longer as CEOs and members of Congress and professors because they are remaining sharp and healthy for longer. It’s true that not every job is as glamorous or status-rich as those positions. But that’s life.

Now, what’s true is that despite improved health, there are still many Americans in their late 60s who are genuinely infirm and unable to work.

An unfortunate reality of American life is that our disability income support programs are rather threadbare and poorly designed. What we ought to do is fix this, rather than use untargeted assistance to the elderly as a very expensive substitute. Help those in need, but acknowledge that we can ask more of able-bodied older Americans, whose physical and mental health is better than it’s ever been.

In one sense, this would make the country less of a gerontocracy in the sense that the basic fiscal bargain would be less tilted toward older people. In another, we would be more gerontocratic than ever, with more older people encouraged to hold on to their roles in the workplace and society.

Which I think mostly goes to underscore that it’s an unhelpful term.

When you watch as Lionel Messi competed credibly for the Golden Boot while LeBron James remained a prized free agent for years, both at unprecedentedly advanced ages for high-level athletes, you’re watching extraordinary human achievement, not a nefarious conspiracy of the elderly.

These star athletes are outliers, but so were their predecessors as star athletes. The curve of age and performance is shifting quite broadly, so the outliers — whether in sports or politics or business — are just somewhat more visible. And though there are some adjustments that need to be made as a result, the basic pattern is fundamentally benign and, in fact, worthy of celebration.

item.title: You don’t actually want to buy a house
item.description: The American dream... or just good marketing?
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Once a month, Matt and I do a book club episode of The Argument podcast. In an upcoming episode this month, we are reading Bowling Alone by Robert Putnam. Read along if you are interested, and please comment with any questions or ideas you would like us to explore!

As soon as I began writing publicly about housing policy, people began to ask me for real estate advice. Should I refinance my mortgage? Is it a good time to buy a condo in Northeast D.C.? Am I too young to buy a house?

I have always emphasized that I am not in the business of giving personal financial advice. But I do, unsurprisingly, have a few strongly held views.

To put it glibly, I’m anti-homeownership.

To put it slightly less glibly, I think that the bipartisan cult of homeownership — a cult that urges people to go all in on one immovable, nondiversified asset in hopes that they will be able to sell it at just the right moment to finance their retirement — is extremely irresponsible.

Share

If you want to buy a house as a matter of consumption, have at it. If I were wealthy, I would definitely find it fun to outfit a house to my exacting, idiosyncratic preferences. But so many people are invested in convincing you that it is always the correct financial decision to buy rather than rent.

David Bach, author of The Automatic Millionaire, an incredibly popular personal finance book that achieved global reach after being launched on The Oprah Winfrey Show in 2004, argued that “the most important advice I can tell you right now if you’re young is: Don’t listen to these people that tell you should [sic] rent versus buy .”

Perhaps the media’s most popular financial-advice personality is Dave Ramsey, who treats the choice to rent as a temporary state for people who are either in debt or haven’t saved up enough for a down payment.

In politics, then-President George W. Bush proclaimed that “we want everybody in America to own their own home.”

But I’m not buying it.

I probably don’t have to quote all these people because you, like me, have probably been at the receiving end of familial and public pressure to become a homeowner. And while a home is a legitimate consumption choice and sometimes a good investment, let me reiterate: It is an irresponsible public message to treat a leveraged, nondiversified, illiquid asset as the universally correct foundation for personal financial security.

My skepticism toward the cult of homeownership stems from two beliefs:

First, the best personal financial advice is to diversify your assets. And not only is a home a single asset, it is also tied closely to your employment prospects. If, for instance, there’s a local labor market shock — like the president of the United States empowering the world’s richest man to illegally fire employees of your region’s largest employer — that blow to your job opportunities is going to correlate with home prices in your area also going down.

As a result, instead of an asset that’s there for you when other things are going poorly, a home is an asset that is likely to perform poorly exactly when you need it not to.

Second is the belief is that people severely underrate the benefits of mobility in maintaining financial security. Owning a home makes it much harder to leave your region if you need to. When you lose your job — or just want a new one — homeownership acts as a drag. Two economists argued in a 2024 paper that it contributes to “lower migration to better job markets.”

Subscribe now

The cult of homeownership can have disastrous policy consequences. If politicians believe that promoting homeownership is an overriding concern, they do things like sell houses in floodplains to low-income homebuyers.

When pressed about this practice during the Biden administration, a Department of Housing and Urban Development spokesperson argued that “locking low-income homebuyers out of a great number of affordable homeownership opportunities because the homes are located in communities within flood zones not only runs contrary to the Administration’s objectives of achieving greater equity in homeownership, but prohibiting sales based on income would be comparable to sanctioning a resurgence of redlining.”

You heard that right: It is redlining not to sell a home to a first-time homebuyer in a floodplain.

Matt, who owns not one but two homes, is much less convinced of my anti-homeownership agenda. While he agrees that homes aren’t fantastic investments — and that in an ideal world, we would change a lot about American homeownership policy — he thinks that the way homeownership forces savings is reason enough to recommend it to people in general. (Allow me to reiterate that none of this is personal financial advice.)

Watch or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

The Argument. Libbing out.

The transcript will be after the paywall in this post for paying subscribers.

item.title: Young people like journalism, just not enough to consume it
item.description: Young people are weirdly chill about the media
item.content:encoded:
By John Robert Thomason

I was recently delighted to discover that my fellow Americans do not consider me an elite.

In The Argument’s recent poll of registered voters, fielded nationally between July 20 and 26, 2026, we asked respondents who they considered elite.

Of all the groups we listed, journalists were tied as the least selected group at just 9%.

As someone entering middle age and therefore excessively concerned with what young people think of my kind, I eagerly checked the breakdown of the results by age and discovered that just 7% of the youths (18- to 29-year-olds) consider journalists to be elites.

Young people actually have a more favorable view of journalists than any other age cohort. With 57% of 18- to 29-year-olds viewing us positively, my colleagues are more popular than Democrats, Republicans, billionaires, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. (We do, somewhat vexingly, remain less popular than college professors.)

Share

It’s hard to see young people’s attitudes as especially informed since, according to them, they simply do not read or watch the news very much — at least not without the mediation of social media.

Regular consumption of traditional news sources — by which I mean newspapers, news websites, and television — declines dramatically as you climb down the age ladder. Those under the age of 30 are less than half as likely to get regular news from TV as the general population and 8 percentage points less likely to read newspapers and news websites regularly.

Of all the traditional formats, newspapers and websites are the most used by 18- to 29-year-olds — but with just 33% of this group perusing these sources regularly, they are still distinctly unpopular parts of their news diet, on par with Elon Musk’s X. Compare that with TikTok, podcasts/YouTube, and Instagram, where 42% to 53% of young people say they get their news.

Subscribe now

Even Facebook is slightly more popular than traditional news sources, although at 36%, the youngest subgroup’s rate of regular Facebook usage is about the same as that for our age 65 and over respondents, with whom Facebook is the most popular social media news source by far.

Young people probably don’t see themselves as opting out of news consumption: Only 4% selected “none of the above” when we asked for their news sources, in line with the general population.

And, just like older voters, the 18-to-29 cohort has opinions on bias and partisanship in journalism — albeit distinct ones. While nearly half of our respondents overall think that journalists have a liberal bias, only 40% of those under 30 feel the same. This shift is primarily accounted for by a larger proportion of 18- to 29-year-olds saying that journalists are “neither more liberal nor more conservative” than any other age group.

There are a couple reasons this may be the case.

  1. Our 18- to 29-year-old respondents were 15 percentage points more liberal than our sample overall, so they may be less likely to see liberal bias than a more conservative overall population.

  2. Younger respondents, who consume primarily algorithmic media, may be working off an implicit redefinition of what a journalist actually is. After all, is a gonzo YouTuber named Reckless Ben who’s obsessed with catching an alleged Lego thief a liberal or a conservative? I can’t even venture a guess.

But as to whether or not the traditional national media are “fair and unbiased,” all age groups are split roughly 50/50. That said, there is a dramatic drop-off from the 18% of those 65 or over who believe the news can be trusted “most or all of the time” to the merely 8% of those under 45 who believe the same.

This is directionally consistent with 2025 results from Gallup, which found a 15-point gap in trust in mass media between 18- to 29-year-olds and those 65 and over — a gap that has widened dramatically since the 2001 to 2003 period when the two were at parity.

In some ways, this all confirms what we already know: We are entering a world where information delivery is increasingly fragmented and traditional gatekeeping institutions have diminished trust and influence. This has created formidable challenges for the news business and will continue to do so.

But, to the extent our survey results offer any solace, it seems like America’s young adults are approaching the field with a slightly more open mind than older Americans. And they are not particularly buying the “liberal media” narrative that the right has been pushing to discredit the profession since before they were born.
